---

That last afternoon of skipping stones—watching the river-glass craze and scatter—was the closest the two brothers ever came to one another. They knotted their lines in tight lockstitch, split what they'd caught, and cooked a modest supper on sticks over the fire. By dawn, the older brother had taken to hurling whatever bottle fragments and oyster shells he could scavenge across the water. Then the younger boy, high-voiced still, let out a cry that seemed to darken the very river. Lord, the sound that rose from him carried so far it carved itself into all of us who heard it—and it has clung ever since.

Hadn't they clung just as fiercely themselves—tooth and claw, to branch and bark—before the man arrived with his truck to take them away? They were driven off, some say, to somewhere upcountry, further inland. Where exactly they ended up, or why, no one but the brothers themselves ever knew. And no one but them could say how they later made their way back—what roads they walked, what woods they crossed, which creeks they forded, which trains they caught, or who, if anyone, lent them aid along the way.

They did come home safely, in the end. But they came home hollow—blank as empty houses. They returned as one brother, and then the other—yet never again, in any way that mattered, as *themselves*.

# The Last Morning by the River

The evening began as so many others had—two brothers, bound by blood and circumstance, finding their way to the water's edge one final time. They skipped flat stones across the current's surface, watching them dance and dive beneath the darkening sky, each throw perhaps carrying more weight than either boy could name. Later, they built a small fire and speared what food they had onto sticks, letting the flames do their slow, honest work. It was a supper of simple things—smoke, char, and the quiet companionship that only siblings who have weathered something together can share. Neither spoke of what was coming. Perhaps neither fully understood it themselves.

When dawn broke gray and cool over the river, something shifted. The older brother, in what might have been ritual or rage or grief too large for words, began hurling fragments of broken bottles and brittle oyster shells out across the water. Each piece caught the weak morning light before vanishing beneath the surface with a sound like small, sharp punctuation marks. The younger brother's response was different—guttural, involuntary. He let loose a cry that seemed to come from somewhere beneath language altogether, a sound so raw and piercing that it lodged itself in the memory of everyone within earshot. Those who heard it would later struggle to describe it, reaching for words like *animal* or *unearthly*, settling on none of them completely.

Then came the truck, and the man who drove it. He arrived without ceremony, loaded the brothers in, and drove them away from the river, away from the fire's last embers, away from everything familiar. Word passed quietly afterward that he'd taken them upcountry, inland, toward some destination that remained frustratingly vague in every retelling.

What happened between that departure and their eventual return exists now only as absence—a gap in the story that no one has ever managed to fill. Which roads carried them? What woods did they pass through, what creeks did they ford, what trains might have rattled beneath them in the dark? Did strangers help them along the way, offering rides or directions or simple kindness? The details have been lost, swallowed by time and silence, leaving behind only the fact of their absence and, eventually, the fact of their return.

For they did come home. Their bodies walked back through the door, breathing, upright, technically whole. But something essential had been left behind on that journey, or perhaps taken from them along the way. The brothers who returned were not the brothers who had left. They moved through the world as familiar shapes—same faces, same names, same blood—but hollowed out somehow, present in body while absent in every other way that mattered. Whatever animated them before, whatever spark had made them *themselves*, seemed to have been extinguished somewhere in that unmapped stretch between the river and home.
outputs.L4:
# The River Remembers What We Cannot Say

The morning mist still clung to the water when Tomás found his brother sitting on the flat gray stone, the one shaped like a sleeping turtle, where they had sat a thousand mornings before. Elias didn't look up. He was skipping stones, watching them kiss the surface twice, three times, before sinking into the current that had raised them both.

"You're up early," Tomás said, settling beside him. The stone was cold through his trousers, but he didn't mind. Six years separated them—Tomás the elder, Elias still soft-cheeked with childhood—but the river made such distinctions meaningless. Here, they were simply brothers.

"Couldn't sleep." Elias picked up another stone, weighed it in his palm. "Mama was crying again last night."

Tomás said nothing. There was nothing to say that would make the debts disappear, that would bring back what the drought had taken, that would soften the hard lines that had settled into their father's face like cracks in dry earth.

Instead, he reached over and messed his brother's hair, the way he'd done since Elias was small enough to carry on his shoulders. Elias swatted his hand away, laughing despite himself, and for a moment—just a moment—the weight of everything lifted. They were only boys by a river, watching light fracture on water, arguing about whether the fish were biting or sulking in the deeper pools.

"Race you to the bend," Elias said suddenly, already scrambling up.

"You always lose."

"Not always." 

They ran along the bank, bare feet finding familiar paths between roots and stones, laughter echoing off water they'd known their whole lives. This river had taught them to swim, had cooled them through summers that stretched endless and golden, had witnessed every secret they'd ever whispered to each other in the dark.

Neither of them heard the truck until it was already there.

---

The man who emerged wore a uniform they didn't recognize, insignia unfamiliar, boots too clean for someone claiming official business. He spoke their names as if reading them from a list, though neither brother remembered giving their names to anyone.

"Come with me," he said, and it wasn't a request.

Tomás remembers reaching for Elias's hand—remembers that much clearly—but the memory blurs after that, fractures like light through disturbed water. There were other children in the truck bed, huddled and silent, eyes hollow with a fear too large for their small faces. Someone was crying. Someone else had stopped crying long before, had gone somewhere internal where tears no longer reached.

The road stretched inland, away from everything they knew. Mountains they'd only seen as blue shadows on the horizon grew close, then closer, then swallowed them whole. Days blurred into weeks. There were buildings with no windows, men who spoke in clipped voices, work that broke small bodies and smaller spirits. There were nights when Tomás held his brother close, both of them pretending sleep while listening to sounds neither wanted to name.

What happened in those months—or was it years?—exists now only in fragments, the way dreams dissolve upon waking, leaving only impressions: cold, hunger, the particular quality of silence that follows violence. Neither brother speaks of it, not to each other, not to anyone. Some things cannot survive translation into words. They can only be carried, like stones in the pocket, forever weighing down the one who bears them.

---

The road home revealed itself slowly, in pieces, the way a puzzle assembles without a clear picture to guide it. A kind stranger. A stolen ride on a produce truck. Days walking through unfamiliar terrain, following rivers because rivers, they both remembered, eventually led somewhere.

They didn't speak of what had happened. They didn't speak of much at all.

When they finally crossed back into familiar territory—recognized a particular hill, a certain bend in a dirt road, the specific quality of light that meant home—neither brother felt the relief they'd once imagined they would feel. They had rehearsed this moment during their captivity, had held it like a talisman against despair: the return, the reunion, the restoration of everything stolen from them.

But standing at the edge of their village, watching smoke curl from familiar chimneys, they felt strangely disconnected, as if watching someone else's homecoming from a great distance.

Their mother wept when she saw them—wept and held them and touched their faces as if verifying their solidity, their realness. Their father, usually so contained, could not speak at all, just gripped them both in an embrace that lasted longer than any embrace they remembered from before.

The village celebrated. Neighbors brought food, embraces, tears of relief. The brothers who had been lost were found. The story would be told and retold, softened at its edges, transformed into something bearable for those who needed to believe that suffering has a redemptive shape, that lost things can be simply restored.

But Tomás and Elias knew better now. They smiled when expected, ate what was placed before them, allowed themselves to be embraced and celebrated and wept over. Yet something essential had been extracted during those months inland, something that could not be returned no matter how far they'd walked, no matter how many rivers they'd followed home.

---

Sometimes, in the early morning mist, Tomás returns to the flat gray stone shaped like a sleeping turtle. He sits where he once sat with his brother, watching water move past exactly as it always has, indifferent to human suffering, indifferent to time itself.

Elias no longer skips stones. He sits very still, watching the current, as if searching for something he lost within its depths—some earlier version of himself that existed before the truck, before the buildings with no windows, before he learned what silence could mean.

They are brothers still. They share blood, shared history, the same childhood bedroom with its cracked window and creaking floorboards. But the boys who once raced along this riverbank, who argued about fish and laughed without weight, without shadow—those boys did not return with them.

What came back instead were careful approximations, bodies that moved through familiar spaces performing familiar gestures, while something essential remained elsewhere, lost among mountains that had taught them lessons no child should learn. They looked like themselves. They answered to their names. But their mother, in her quietest moments, sometimes looked at her sons with an expression of profound confusion, as if recognizing that while their faces remained the same, something behind their eyes had fundamentally changed.

The river continued its eternal movement, indifferent to all of this, carrying water toward the sea exactly as it had before, exactly as it would continue long after both brothers were gone, long after anyone remembered their names or their story or the particular quality of loss that had transformed two ordinary boys into something else entirely—present in body, absent in ways too profound to name, forever altered by roads they never chose to walk.

# The Lord Carved

In the quiet hours before dawn, when shadows still clung to the corners of the workshop, the old carpenter would begin his work. His hands, weathered by decades of labor, moved with practiced precision across the grain of ancient oak. Some said he carved not merely wood, but stories—each groove and curve telling a tale only he could fully understand.

The villagers called him "the Lord" not for any noble birth, but for the reverence with which he approached his craft. To him, carving was not simply cutting away excess material; it was an act of discovery, of revealing what already existed within the wood, waiting patiently to be found.

"The Lord carved as though in prayer," an old woman once remarked, watching him work through the workshop window. There was truth in her words. Each stroke of his chisel seemed deliberate, almost sacred, as if he were uncovering something eternal hidden beneath the rough exterior of raw timber.

His creations filled the small chapel at the edge of town—wooden saints with serene expressions, doves caught mid-flight, intricate patterns that seemed to shift and breathe in candlelight. Children would press their small hands against the smooth surfaces, marveling at how something once so ordinary as a fallen branch could become so extraordinary.

When asked about his gift, the carpenter would simply smile and say that he was merely a vessel. The true artistry, he believed, belonged to something greater—a divine hand guiding his own, whispering shapes and forms into existence through the humble medium of wood and steel.

Long after his passing, his carvings remained throughout the village, silent testaments to a life devoted to transforming the ordinary into the sacred, one careful cut at a time.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an experimental prose-poem about two brothers separated by force and their strange journey home, using fragmented syntax and dashes.
counterfactuals.output:
**Two Rivers, One Mouth**

—the truck took him first, the younger one, the one with the gap tooth and the habit of counting stars through fence-wire—took him east while the other—older, quieter, the one who memorized his brother's laugh so he could return it later—was left holding a shoe, just one, small, still warm—

*where does a body go when it is halved—*

—years move like this: a train that doesn't stop, only slows enough to throw you off—each stop a country wearing a different mother's face—he learned to sleep standing, learned the particular silence of borders, how guards ask questions already answered by your clothes—

—the younger one grew up in rooms that were never square, always someone else's corners—he kept the gap tooth, kept counting, but the stars became streetlights, became the small orange eyes of stopped cars—he did not know his own age some years, guessed it by the length of his hunger—

—the older one walked. Not always forward. Sometimes in circles that felt like prayer, sometimes toward smoke because smoke means someone is still cooking, still living, still—

*brother, are you the smoke or the fire that made it—*

—they say the body remembers what the mind forgets—so when the older one crossed a checkpoint and heard, three tents down, someone humming a tune their mother sang wrong on purpose to make them laugh—he stopped—he did not breathe—he thought: *this is either God or grief playing tricks, and I no longer care which—*

—the younger one was already walking toward the sound of his own name, mispronounced in the older one's mouth for twenty years, still recognizable, still his—

—they did not run. Neither had the legs for it anymore. They walked the way old water walks—slow, insistent, unstoppable—until the distance was just the width of two open arms, then the width of a held breath, then nothing—

*this is not an ending—this is a wound closing wrong, beautifully wrong, scar-shaped like a map home—*

—home: not a house. Not a country. Just this—two heartbeats finally in the same weather, two shadows finally overlapping at dusk—

—the shoe, still in the older one's bag all these years, still warm somehow, still fits—

—they do not speak for a long time. They do not need to. The silence between brothers who have survived the same forgetting is its own language, is dashes strung together forever—is continuing—is continuing—is—
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a piece of literary flash fiction with a rural, dialect-inflected voice, involving a truck taking children away and them finding their way back changed.
counterfactuals.output:
**What the Truck Brung Back**

The truck come every seventh year, gray as a dead tooth, and it took the children the week after harvest when the roads was hard enough to bear the weight. Nobody remembered who sent for it. Ma Odell said her granny didn't remember neither, said it was just a thing that come, like frost, like the whip-poor-will callin before rain.

They'd load up six, seven young'uns at a time, the ones turned eight that year, and the truck'd grind off down Coal Holler Road with its taillights bleedin red through the dust, and that was that. We didn't ask where. Askin never brung nobody back sooner.

They was gone three weeks that time. My brother Dillard went, and Ruthie Combs, and the Pruitt twins who couldn't hardly be told apart even by their own mama. I was six and too young yet, and I recall standin at the fence line every evenin watchin the road like watchin a pot that won't boil.

When the truck come back it come back slower, like it was carryin somethin heavier than it left with, though it was the same six children in the bed of it, wrapped in the same wool blankets.

They didn't run to their mamas like children ought. They climbed down one by one, quiet-like, and stood in a row same as they'd been taught to stand for pictures at the county fair, and they looked at us with eyes gone the color of creek water after a hard rain — not brown no more, not blue, just clouded over with somethin none of us had a name for.

Dillard didn't speak for two days. When he did speak it was to tell me the names of stars I never heard tell of, said 'em soft in his sleep like he was prayin to 'em. Ruthie Combs took to walkin the fence line at night, countin her steps out loud in a language that wasn't English and wasn't nothin else neither, till her mama took to lockin the door.

The Pruitt twins could finish each other's sentences before, but after, they didn't talk to nobody but each other, and not out loud. They'd just look, and one would nod like the other'd said somethin, and go on about their chores.

Preacher Hobbs said it was the Devil's work. Old Ma Odell said it was worse — said it was learnin, and learnin always costs somethin, and children ought never be sent off to get it for free.

I asked Dillard once, years on, what they done to him out there past the ridge. He was near grown by then, married to Ruthie Combs as it happened, the two of 'em drawn together like they'd shared some secret the rest of us couldn't ever get told.

He looked at me a long while with them clouded eyes, and he said, "They didn't do nothin to us, Ellis. They just showed us how big it all is."

"How big what is?"

"Everything," he said, and went back to shellin his corn, and wouldn't say no more.

The seventh year come round again and the truck come gray and groanin down Coal Holler Road, and this time I was of age, eight years old exact, and they put me in the bed of it alongside Sary Gentry and the youngest Ostrander boy, wrapped me in a wool blanket smelled of mothballs and somethin underneath like ozone after lightning.

I won't tell you what's past the ridge. I don't recall bein asked not to — I just find I can't. The words won't come to where my mouth can shape 'em, like tryin to hold water in a fist.

But I'll tell you this: I come back with eyes the color of creek water, and I count my steps some nights without meanin to, and I know the names of stars my own granny never heard tell of.

And when my boy turned eight, and the truck come gray and grindin down the holler, I stood at the fence same as my mama stood, and I did not weep, though I wanted to.

Because I knew, same as she must've known, that he'd come back different, and he'd come back quiet, and he'd come back *bigger* somehow, in a place the truck could never put back small again.

That's the cost, I reckon. That's always been the cost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a short lyrical narrative in the style of Cormac McCarthy, using unconventional punctuation and invented compound words, about siblings skipping rocks before being taken away.
counterfactuals.output:
The river ran the color of old nickels that evening and the two of them stood at its edge like something not yet named by God. The boy stooping to find the flat ones the good ones the skipstones worn smooth by a thousand years of water not caring. His sister watching him with her arms crossed against the coming cold.

He'd cock his arm back and let fly and the stone would skitter cross that dark water leaving little bloomrings that spread and died and spread and died again into nothing. Four skips. Five. Once six and he turned to see had she seen and she had.

Your turn, he said.

She shook her head. Not tonight.

Behind them up the bank the house sat dark already though the sun had not yet gone down full behind the ridgeline. No lamplight in the windows. No smoke from the chimney. The truck would come at dark they'd been told. The truck would come and take them to the place with the other children the greyfaced woman had spoken of in her flat voice that carried no more feeling than the water carried memory of the stones that vanished in it.

He handed her a stone anyway. Flat and gray and fitting her palm like it had been made for just that hand.

Just once, he said.

She turned it in her fingers. This river, she said. It dont know were leaving.

It dont know nothing, he said. Thats how come it can hold so much.

She wound up then and threw and the stone went out low and skipping once twice three times before it caught some current beneath the surface and dropped from sight like it had never been thrown at all like the throwing and the dropping were the same single act unbroken by time.

They stood there watching the place where it went down. The lastlight going purple on the water. Somewhere back of them a screen door somewhere a voice already calling their names into the dusk though it was not yet dark enough for the world to swallow them. Not yet. Not just yet.

He picked up one more stone. Best one yet, he said. You want it?

She looked at it in his hand. Save it, she told him. For when we get back.

He put it in his pocket without a word and they walked on up toward the house and whatever waited on beyond it in the shape of doors closing and roads unwinding into a country neither one of them had asked to be born to nor now had any say in leaving.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Give me an abstract, poetic vignette about loss of innocence, using bullet-point fragments, archaic diction, and a haunting refrain about brothers returning "not them."
counterfactuals.output:
# What the Orchard Kept

*a vignette*

- Once there were two boys who ran as one shadow beneath the apple boughs
- Once there was a war that ate the summer whole
- The letters came, then did not come, then came again in a stranger's hand

— *and the brothers came home, but not them, never them* —

- Behold: the eldest's eyes, once quick as sparrows, now still as winter ponds
- Behold: the youngest's laugh, that silver bell, gone tarnished, gone to rust
- Mark how the mother sets two plates from habit, and weeps into the third
- Mark how the dog will not approach the one who wears his master's face

— *for the brothers came home, but not them, never them* —

- Thou orchard, dost thou remember the boys who stole thy fruit unpunished?
- Thou river, dost thou recall the ones who dared thy currents laughing?
- The trees say nothing. The water keeps its secrets. The world moves on, indifferent to what was borrowed and not returned
- What marched away as innocence returned as something wearing innocence's old coat

— *and the brothers came home, but not them, never them* —

- Let it be known: some doors, once opened, cannot close the same
- Let it be known: some boys who leave as boys return as monuments to boys
- The village bells rang welcome. The village bells rang wrong.
- Somewhere still, beneath old boughs, two shadow-children run forever uncaught, forever unaged, forever *before*

— *while the brothers, the brothers, came home— but not them, never them, never them again* —
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a stream-of-consciousness micro-story with a Southern Gothic feel, focusing on sound, memory, and transformation after a childhood trauma involving separation and return.
counterfactuals.output: The cicadas start up around six and Mama used to say that's the sound of the dead clearing their throats, getting ready to talk, and I believed her the way you believe things at eight years old, whole and unquestioning, before the truck came down Route 9 and took me somewhere with fluorescent lights that hummed a different song entirely, no cicadas there, just the hum and the squeak of shoes on linoleum and a woman named Dr. Ferris asking do you remember your mother's face and I said yes but I was lying because already it was going soft at the edges like a photograph left in a windowsill, sun-bleached, and three years is a long time when you're small, three years is long enough for a whole house to grow up around your absence the way kudzu grows over a barn until you can't tell what shape it used to be, and when they brought me back—not to her, she was gone by then, gone the way that means dead but nobody says the word to a child, they just say gone and let you fill in the rest with your own private mythology—I stood in the yard and heard the cicadas again, the same throat-clearing hum, and it was like time had folded over on itself like a dog-eared page, like I'd never left except everything had left me, the house sagging, paint gone to gray, and my aunt saying you've gotten so tall, honey, like height was the only transformation that mattered, like I hadn't grown a whole new skin in that other place, hard and shiny as a beetle's back, and that night the cicadas kept on and on and I lay in the bed that used to be mine, in a room that smelled like dust and old rain, and I thought: this is what the dead sound like when they're trying to tell you something and you don't have the ears for it yet, and I closed my eyes and let the hum come up through the floorboards, through the mattress, into the marrow, until I couldn't tell if it was the bugs singing or my own blood finally remembering the shape of this particular darkness, this particular home, this particular grief that had been waiting on me, patient as kudzu, patient as August, to come back and be swallowed whole.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
